checks: Fatou is applied on the limiting body's interior, whose points eventually belong to the current bodies. The affine limits are nonnegative on K. If any vanishes at an interior point it vanishes identically and forces the limiting minimum to be identically zero, contradicting inverse integrability. A constant limiting plane is thus strictly positive.

Distinct affine planes have volume-null ties, so discarding them and retaining the exact active cell preserves the per-cell inverse bound. Its anchor can lie on the boundary since convexity alone yields the slice inclusion. The factor b/(b-s) turns the containment into exact nesting.

Coarea in orthogonal coordinates contributes 1/|c_j|, and the reciprocal density converts |ds|/s to dr/lambda_j. Strictly below the start level no slice exists. Strictly above it s_j/b_j vanishes uniformly on compact rate intervals, including when the anchor height tends to zero.

The projected Jacobian is bounded by 2^(d-1) on the integration interval q to r_0. Its mass estimate holds at each r≥r_0 by nesting; q=r_0/2 gives the stated 2^d bound for a fixed positive-height affine anchor.

Helly selection with a countable dense set of tests produces a single exceptional countable set and weak finite limits, with right limits preserving monotonicity. Projection and physical-coordinate errors vanish uniformly on compact positive-rate ranges above the start. Dominated convergence identifies the disintegration of the given weak limit.

Brunn–Minkowski applies to the input intersections with the projected convex slice. Inner approximation and open-input/closed-target Portmanteau estimates retain the 1/(d−1) inequality for positive masses without requiring an ambient limiting density. The geometric-mean inequality and the support arguments then give log-concavity and nesting.

Source 1ec792c66c5ddc47 §§1–4 and §8 (15)–(17) cover the fixed-anchor and delayed geometric-cell statements. Neither the original nor the draft extends the conclusion to arbitrary source labels or removes a possible threshold atom by slicing alone.

dependencies.hypotheses: Applied in dimension d−1≥1 to compact measurable input subsets of a projected convex slice; their Minkowski combination is compact and remains in that convex slice.
dependencies.reference: R. J. Gardner, The Brunn–Minkowski Inequality, Theorem 4.1

overlap.comparison: This fact supplies weak Brunn–Minkowski closure for common-scale cuts, and in the single-base case overlaps the fixed-rate closure step. It assumes the weak slice limits; it gives no positive-rate coarea disintegration, projective nesting, local mass bound, or delayed-start geometry.
It identifies the positive-rate residual in a joint surface lift under separate compactness hypotheses. It does not give a conditional inverse law or its tangential shape.

readability: The t in the projective inclusion is an affine level, and r is its inverse logarithmic rate. The threshold exclusion and the possibility of mass exactly at the threshold are correctly separated.
review_method: Independent cold read of the frozen theorem and proof, source-locator and dependency comparison at the pinned graph, and exact arithmetic on the illustrative constructions where relevant.
summary: The actual affine coarea law and the radial projection about a cell anchor give the stated measure-valued monotonicity and fixed-rate concavity. The argument allows collapsing tangential supports and leaves the single start rate open.
